extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, hyperlocal media practitioners, and local journalists seeking audience-centred insight
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and descriptive standards for what makes content 'newsworthy' or 'shareworthy' on hyperlocal Facebook Pages, based on ethnographic observation of audience practices and platform metrics. Useful for assessing/crafting local posts that prompt sourcing, sharing, or civic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional newsworthiness / news values (Galtung & Ruge; Harcup & O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events must meet established criteria to ‘become’ news in producers' eyes; classic news values (e.g., prominence, conflict, human interest) determine what mainstream news treats as newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that many traditional criteria still apply to online sharing (Trilling et al. 2017). Use these values to predict attention, but be aware they interact with platform and audience dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability / Shareworthiness (audience perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension of newsworthiness emphasising whether audiences will source, cite, comment on, endorse and share stories online; a distinct way of observing the value of news to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate content not only for journalistic importance but for whether audience members will identify with it, find it worth the extra labour to share, and judge it appropriate for their local social space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism / clickbait tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensationalism is defined as the degree to which a story 'adheres to a style (content and form) that seeks to evoke emotion or emulate tabloid-like structures that trivialize the news'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although sensational stories may be shared more on Facebook than non-sensational ones, sensationalism is not necessarily the key driver of sharing; do not rely on trivialization alone to produce shares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness / everyday functional value
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are practically useful or provide immediately actionable information (e.g., traffic delays, bus timetabling, missing pets) are more likely to be shared by audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise immediacy, actionable detail, and local utility when assessing or producing hyperlocal content; these often outperform political/civic posts in reach and clicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability / local-identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that feels 'relatable' — featuring politicians, celebrities, or 'relatable' neighbourhood figures and everyday occurrences — encourages sharing because readers see themselves or their neighbours in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories to foreground local human elements and everyday hooks; even preposterous events can be highly shareable if readers imagine experiencing them locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact & prominence / unusualness
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles with impact, prominence, or unusual news values (e.g., unusual, prominent events) prompt sharing — García-Perdomo et al. (2018) found these led to more Facebook shares than Twitter shares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a story has measurable impact or prominence for the local audience; unusual events can be highlighted but balance with practical relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediacy / time-sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate, real-time information (e.g., live updates, traffic incidents) attracts higher reach and clicks compared to scheduled or less time-sensitive civic posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Facebook's affordances for rapid posting to share time-sensitive local updates; audiences value immediacy in hyperlocal spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visuals increase engagement (images/photos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Posts that include images (e.g., photos of lost pets) generate higher user engagement and shares according to both the chapter's examples and cited studies (Bonsón et al. 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear images where appropriate to increase likelihood of shares and clicks—especially for appeals and lost/found items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calls to action / calculable goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Posts with a clear, calculable goal (e.g., find a lost dog, witness appeal) and where individuals can contribute with little effort are more likely to be shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the desired action explicit and easy; audiences share when they see a direct, achievable way to help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story types / Visitor Posts typology
rubrics_metrics.description: A typology of audience-sourced story types observed in 310 Visitor Posts: Appeals, Reports, Questions, Events as dominant categories; plus Promotions, Rants, Thanks, Offers of help, Congratulations in the tail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and encourage these normative post types in hyperlocal Pages; Appeals and Reports tend to be more effortful and share-inducing than Questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience sourcing and participation norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members actively source and suggest stories, observing informal norms about what is 'appropriate' to post; this collective practice shapes what is proposed for reposting by editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design community spaces and moderation to surface useful Visitor Posts; recognise that observed norms will evolve and can create feedback loops (e.g., many lost-pet posts encouraging more of the same).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial control and curation (hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook Page administrators ultimately control what is posted to the Page's main stream and curate content—deciding what Visitor Posts to repost and when to steer the Page away from dominant trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should monitor audience sourcing, Insights, and community effects, and actively curate to align content with the Page's aims (e.g., reduce overabundance of one story type).

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform metrics for evaluating attractiveness (Facebook Insights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measures used: Reach (number seeing the post), Post Clicks, Reactions (comments, shares); these indicate what the audience finds attractive or valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these metrics to compare post performance (e.g., bus timetabling post reached 11,000 with high clicks/shares) but interpret alongside qualitative community feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention shares / tagging as targeted sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of typing a friend's name into comments to notify them ('mention shares') is used to draw specific people to a story, organise attendance, or pass relevant local information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise tagging as a low-effort, targeted sharing mechanism that extends reach within local social networks—design posts that invite or facilitate mention-sharing when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clicktivism as an engagement anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Clicks, Likes, and Shares may not translate into offline action (e.g., volunteer event with many likes but few attendees), reflecting 'clicktivist' behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat high online engagement as necessary but not sufficient for offline mobilisation; where attendance/action is needed, reinforce with reminders and multiple channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience demographics shape content preference
rubrics_metrics.description: The user base demographics (e.g., 2:1 female:male, 93% 25+ in WV11) influence what stories are requested, sourced, and shared (family events, lost pet appeals, neighbourhood complaints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and monitor your Page's demographic profile to tailor content to the community's likely interests and needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium/format accessibility affects consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Format accessibility (online immediacy vs print distribution constraints) influences whether local people use a source; online hyperlocal Pages can be more accessible than print newspapers for many residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose delivery formats that match audience routines and access patterns; online posting can increase visibility and responsiveness relative to periodic print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap of local information ecologies (multi-source constellations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences operate within overlapping communicative spaces (mainstream outlets, councils, police, local groups); content may be encountered via following a Page or reposts from neighbouring Pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate and be aware of neighbouring Pages and local information sources; reposting from relevant sources can increase usefulness but editors should credit sources and maintain curation standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnographic depth / embeddedness as method for judging value
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep, longitudinal engagement with audiences reveals what they find valuable (their everyday practices, media ecologies, and the ‘lived experience’ context for sharing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating shareworthiness, combine metrics with qualitative, embedded observation or interviews to understand motivations beyond surface indicators.
